title: EntireFunction
content: An entire function is represented as a structure carrying its power series coefficients $a_n$ with the constraint that infinitely many are nonzero (ruling out polynomials). This captures the essential property: the power series converges on all of $\mathbb{C}$, and the function has infinitely many terms contributing to its growth.
mathContext: $f(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n z^n$ where $\forall N,\; \exists n > N,\; a_n \neq 0$. The condition ensures $f$ is transcendental entire, not a polynomial.

title: maxTerm (μ)
content: The maximum term $\mu(r)$ is the supremum of $|a_n| r^n$ over all $n$. For entire functions, this is well-defined and finite for each $r > 0$. It measures how large the dominant individual term of the power series can be at radius $r$, ignoring cancellations between terms.
mathContext: $\mu(r) = \sup_{n \ge 0} |a_n| r^n$. For transcendental entire functions, $\mu(r) \to \infty$ as $r \to \infty$, and the index achieving the supremum (the central index) also tends to infinity.

title: maxModulus (M)
content: The maximum modulus $M(r)$ is the supremum of $|f(z)|$ over the circle $|z| = r$. By the maximum modulus principle, this equals the supremum over the closed disk $|z| \le r$. This is the standard measure of entire function growth used in Nevanlinna theory and order-type classification.
mathContext: $M(r) = \sup_{|z|=r} |f(z)| = \sup_{\theta \in [0, 2\pi)} \left|\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n (r e^{i\theta})^n\right|$. By the maximum modulus principle, $M(r)$ is attained on $|z| = r$.

title: termModulusRatio
content: The ratio $\mu(r)/M(r)$ measures how well the entire function is approximated by its single largest term. When $\mu(r)/M(r) \to 1$, the function behaves like a monomial at large radii; when $\to 0$, massive cancellation occurs between terms.
mathContext: $\frac{\mu(r)}{M(r)} = \frac{\sup_n |a_n| r^n}{\sup_{|z|=r} |f(z)|}$. Always in $[0, 1]$ since $\mu(r) \le M(r)$ by the triangle inequality.

title: OriginalConjecture
content: Erdős conjectured that if the limit of $\mu(r)/M(r)$ exists as $r \to \infty$, it must be 0. This would mean that for any transcendental entire function with a well-defined asymptotic ratio, the function's growth is never dominated by a single term. The conjecture turned out to be false in a strong sense.
mathContext: $\text{OriginalConjecture}: \forall f \text{ entire},\; \forall L,\; \lim_{r \to \infty} \frac{\mu(r)}{M(r)} = L \implies L = 0$

title: Clunie's Partial Result
content: Clunie proved that Erdős's conjecture is true when restricted to entire functions with non-negative real coefficients ($a_n \ge 0$ for all $n$). For such functions, there is no cancellation between terms on the positive real axis: $f(r) = \sum a_n r^n = M(r)$ for real $r > 0$. The Wiman-Valiron method then shows $\mu(r)/M(r) \to 0$.
mathContext: If $a_n \ge 0$ for all $n$, then $M(r) = f(r) = \sum a_n r^n$ and $\mu(r)/M(r) \to 0$ as $r \to \infty$. The proof uses the fact that the maximum modulus equals the sum of all terms, which grows much faster than any single term.

title: Clunie-Hayman 1964
content: The central result: Clunie and Hayman (1964) constructed, for any prescribed $\lambda \in [0, 1/2]$, an entire function $f$ with $\mu(r)/M(r) \to \lambda$. Their construction uses carefully designed oscillating coefficients that cause partial cancellation on the circle $|z| = r$, reducing the maximum modulus relative to the maximum term by a controlled factor.
mathContext: $\forall \lambda \in [0, 1/2],\; \exists f \text{ entire},\; \lim_{r \to \infty} \frac{\mu(r)}{M(r)} = \lambda$. The interval $[0, 1/2]$ is sharp: no limit $\lambda > 1/2$ is achievable.

title: Upper Bound 1/2
content: The ratio limit can never exceed 1/2. This follows from a classical inequality: the maximum modulus $M(r)$ can be bounded below by an average involving the maximum term, yielding $\mu(r)/M(r) \le 1/2 + o(1)$. The proof uses properties of the central index and the distribution of terms near the maximum.
mathContext: $\forall f \text{ entire},\; \lim_{r \to \infty} \frac{\mu(r)}{M(r)} = L \implies L \le \frac{1}{2}$. The bound is achieved in the limit by specific Clunie-Hayman constructions.

title: Conjecture Disproved
content: The original conjecture is proved false by exhibiting a specific counterexample: take $\lambda = 1/4 \in (0, 1/2]$ in the Clunie-Hayman theorem to get an entire function with $\mu(r)/M(r) \to 1/4 \neq 0$. The proof is a clean application of the existence result followed by contradiction with the conjecture's requirement that the limit be 0.
mathContext: Take $\lambda = 1/4$. By Clunie-Hayman, $\exists f$ with $\mu(r)/M(r) \to 1/4$. If the conjecture held, $1/4 = 0$, contradiction. Hence $\lnot\text{OriginalConjecture}$.

title: AchievableLimits
content: The set of all real numbers $L$ that arise as $\lim_{r \to \infty} \mu(r)/M(r)$ for some entire function $f$. The complete characterization theorem shows this equals the closed interval $[0, 1/2]$.
mathContext: $\text{AchievableLimits} = \{L \in \mathbb{R} \mid \exists f \text{ entire},\; \lim_{r \to \infty} \mu_f(r)/M_f(r) = L\}$

title: Complete Characterization
content: The achievable limits form exactly the closed interval $[0, 1/2]$. The proof is a set extensionality argument: the forward direction uses the upper bound axiom (and a sorry for the non-negativity of ratios); the reverse direction is the Clunie-Hayman existence result. This is the definitive answer to Erdős's question.
mathContext: $\text{AchievableLimits} = [0, 1/2]$. Proof: $L \in \text{AchievableLimits} \iff 0 \le L \le 1/2$, using $\mu(r)/M(r) \ge 0$ and Clunie-Hayman for both directions.

title: centralIndex
content: The central index $\nu(r)$ is the index $n$ at which $|a_n| r^n$ achieves its maximum (the maximum term). As $r$ increases, the dominant term shifts to higher-order coefficients, so $\nu(r)$ increases. This index plays a central role in Wiman-Valiron theory, which approximates entire functions near their maximum modulus.
mathContext: $\nu(r) = \arg\max_n |a_n| r^n$, defined via Classical.choose. For transcendental entire functions, $\nu(r) \to \infty$ as $r \to \infty$.

title: Central Index Unbounded
content: The central index $\nu(r) \to \infty$ as $r \to \infty$. This is a consequence of the function being transcendental: if only finitely many coefficients were nonzero (polynomial), $\nu(r)$ would eventually stabilize. The unboundedness is essential for Wiman-Valiron theory.
mathContext: $\lim_{r \to \infty} \nu(r) = \infty$, formalized as $\text{Tendsto}\;(\text{centralIndex}\;f)\;\text{atTop}\;\text{atTop}$.

title: μ ≤ M
content: The maximum term never exceeds the maximum modulus: $\mu(r) \le M(r)$ for $r > 0$. This follows because evaluating $f$ at a point on $|z| = r$ where $z^n$ is aligned with $a_n$ for the dominant $n$ gives $|f(z)| \ge |a_n r^n| - \text{(other terms)}$, and in the limit $M(r) \ge \mu(r)$. More directly, the triangle inequality gives $\mu(r) \le \sum |a_n| r^n$ while $M(r)$ can exploit cancellations.
mathContext: $\mu(r) = \sup_n |a_n| r^n \le \sup_{|z|=r} |f(z)| = M(r)$ for $r > 0$.

title: IsNormal
content: An entire function is 'normal' if $\mu(r)/M(r) \to 0$ as $r \to \infty$. Most classical entire functions (exp, sin, cos, Airy functions) are normal. The Clunie-Hayman result shows that non-normal functions with well-defined limits form a rich family parametrized by $\lambda \in (0, 1/2]$.
mathContext: $\text{IsNormal}(f) \iff \lim_{r \to \infty} \frac{\mu(r)}{M(r)} = 0$

title: Positive Coeffs Normal
content: Functions with non-negative real coefficients ($a_n \ge 0$) are normal. The proof (marked sorry) would follow from Clunie's result: when all coefficients are non-negative, $f(r) = M(r) = \sum a_n r^n$, so $\mu(r)/M(r) = (\max a_n r^n)/(\sum a_n r^n) \to 0$ since infinitely many terms contribute.
mathContext: If $a_n \ge 0$ for all $n$, then $M(r) = f(r) = \sum a_n r^n$ and $\mu(r)/M(r) = \frac{\max_n a_n r^n}{\sum_n a_n r^n} \to 0$ as $r \to \infty$.

title: Order
content: The order $\rho$ of an entire function measures its growth rate: $\rho = \inf\{\rho' : M(r) \le C \exp(r^{\rho'})\}$. For example, $\exp(z)$ has order 1, polynomials have order 0, and $\exp(\exp(z))$ has infinite order. The order connects to the distribution of zeros via the Hadamard factorization theorem.
mathContext: $\rho(f) = \inf\{\rho \ge 0 : \exists C > 0,\; \forall r > 0,\; M(r) \le C e^{r^\rho}\} = \limsup_{r \to \infty} \frac{\log \log M(r)}{\log r}$

title: Type
content: The type $\sigma$ of an entire function of order $\rho$ provides a finer growth classification: $M(r) \sim C \exp(\sigma r^\rho)$. Functions are classified as minimal type ($\sigma = 0$), mean type ($0 < \sigma < \infty$), or maximal type ($\sigma = \infty$).
mathContext: $\sigma(f, \rho) = \inf\{\sigma \ge 0 : \exists C > 0,\; \forall r > 0,\; M(r) \le C e^{\sigma r^\rho}\} = \limsup_{r \to \infty} \frac{\log M(r)}{r^\rho}$

title: Order Zero Normal
content: Entire functions of order 0 are normal (i.e., $\mu(r)/M(r) \to 0$). These are very slowly growing functions — slower than $\exp(r^\epsilon)$ for any $\epsilon > 0$. The Clunie-Hayman counterexamples necessarily have infinite order, since even order-zero functions satisfy the original conjecture.
mathContext: $\rho(f) = 0 \implies \text{IsNormal}(f)$. Combined with Clunie's positive-coefficient result, this shows the counterexamples must be both oscillating and fast-growing.

title: Exponential Normal
content: The exponential function $e^z = \sum z^n/n!$ is normal: its maximum term satisfies $\mu(r) \sim r^r e^{-r}/\sqrt{2\pi r}$ (Stirling) while $M(r) = e^r$, giving $\mu(r)/M(r) \to 0$. This is a prototypical example of a 'well-behaved' entire function.
mathContext: For $f(z) = e^z$: $\mu(r) = r^{\lfloor r \rfloor}/\lfloor r \rfloor! \sim e^r / \sqrt{2\pi r}$ by Stirling, so $\mu(r)/M(r) = \mu(r)/e^r \sim 1/\sqrt{2\pi r} \to 0$.

title: Pathological Examples
content: For any $\lambda \in (0, 1/2)$, there exist entire functions of infinite order achieving $\mu(r)/M(r) \to \lambda$. The infinite order is necessary: finite-order functions are known to be normal. These pathological examples have highly irregular growth — faster than any $\exp(r^\rho)$ — yet their ratio stabilizes to a precise limit.
mathContext: $\forall \lambda \in (0, 1/2),\; \exists f$ with $\rho(f) = \infty$ (i.e., $\forall \rho > 0,\; \exists r,\; M(r) > e^{r^\rho}$) and $\mu(r)/M(r) \to \lambda$.

title: erdos_227_statement
content: The complete formal statement assembles three results: (1) the original conjecture is false, (2) Clunie's partial result for positive coefficients holds, and (3) the achievable limits are exactly $[0, 1/2]$. The proof chains together original_conjecture_false, clunie_positive_coeffs, and achievable_limits_characterization.
mathContext: $\lnot\text{OriginalConjecture} \land (\forall f \text{ with } a_n \ge 0,\; \lim \mu/M = 0) \land (\text{AchievableLimits} = [0, 1/2])$
